q: What are generics in Go, and how do they differ from using the empty interface (`any`)?
a:
Generics (Go 1.18+) are **type parameters** on functions and types, constrained by interfaces:

```go
func Max[T cmp.Ordered](a, b T) T {
    if a > b {
        return a
    }
    return b
}
```

Main advantage over `any`: **compile-time type safety** with one implementation. With `any` you lose type information — callers need type assertions, mistakes surface as runtime panics, and you can't use operators like `<` or `+`. Values stored in `any` are boxed (possible allocations); generic code keeps concrete types.

Details:
- Constraints: interfaces with methods and/or type sets (`~int | ~float64`), `comparable`, `cmp.Ordered`; `~T` includes named types with underlying `T`.
- Implementation: **GC-shape stenciling** with dictionaries — one instantiation per shape (all pointers share one), so generic method calls through constraints can be slower than hand-written code.
- Limits: no type parameters on methods, no specialization.
- Standard library: `slices`, `maps`, `cmp`, `sync`-style wrappers, range-over-func iterators (`iter.Seq`, 1.23).

Use generics for containers and algorithms; use interfaces when you need behavior polymorphism.
